title: Effect of Artificial Intelligence Convergence Education Using ChatGPT on Computational Thinking of High School Students in Korea
venue: International Journal on Advanced Science, Engineering and Information Technology
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether an AI convergence education program using ChatGPT can improve high school students’ computational thinking (CT) in authentic school settings in Korea. The authors position the study within growing interest in generative AI in education and specifically ask whether integrating an AI chatbot into design-thinking-based, cross-curricular problem-solving activities produces meaningful learning gains compared with more conventional information-seeking tools.

The intervention was a six-session AI convergence education program organized around the design thinking process: empathy, problem definition, idea generation, prototype, and test. Students in the experimental group used ChatGPT as a personalized learning aid during problem-solving activities, while the control group used search engines and literature information services such as Google Scholar and RISS. The curriculum connected AI use with Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), and students worked on real-life problem-solving topics selected from SDG themes. The program included activities such as persona creation, interviews, brainstorming, mind mapping, proposal writing, 3D modeling, feedback, revision, and presentation.

The study involved 95 students from one general high school in Korea, with 53 students in the experimental group and 42 in the control group. The intervention was delivered by the same teacher over six sessions across approximately two to three weeks, using devices such as computers, tablet PCs, and smartphones in a classroom-based school setting. Outcomes were measured using an 18-item Computational Thinking Scale aligned to Korean curriculum goals and covering abstraction, decomposition, algorithmic thinking, evaluation, and generalization.

The main finding is that the ChatGPT-supported group showed statistically significant gains in overall computational thinking and in all five CT subdomains, whereas the control group did not show significant improvement. The authors conclude that AI chatbot-supported AI convergence education can function as a personalized learning aid and improve students’ CT in high school contexts. However, the paper does not study writing feedback on student-authored drafts, does not report prompt design details, and provides little direct evidence about implementation fidelity, usage intensity, or process mechanisms beyond the broad claim that chatbot-supported individualized problem solving helped learning.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed quasi-experimental pre/post comparison in an authentic high school setting with a control group and reported sample sizes/statistical tests, but it does not appear to be a randomized trial and omits key credibility details such as standardized effect sizes and some implementation/fidelity specifics.
impact_tier_rationale: Findings are statistically positive for computational thinking, but the magnitude of impact is unclear because no standardized effect size or confidence interval is reported. The study therefore indicates promising but not precisely quantified impact.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT was used as a conversational problem-solving aid/personalized tutor within a 6-session high-school AI convergence education program. Students used the chatbot during design-thinking activities (empathy, problem definition, idea generation, prototyping, testing) to ask questions, explore SDG-related topics, and receive iterative support while developing project proposals and 3D-modeled solutions.

Comparator condition in which students completed the same AI convergence/design-thinking curriculum but used search engines and literature information services rather than ChatGPT for information gathering and problem solving.

finding.finding_summary: In a quasi-experimental study of Korean high school students (experimental n=53; control n=42; total n=95), the ChatGPT-supported AI convergence education group showed a significant pre-post gain in computational thinking, increasing from M=3.63 (SD=0.76) to M=4.28 (SD=0.67), t=-4.38, p<.001. The control group using search/literature tools did not significantly improve (M=3.68 to 3.85, t=1.00, p=.32), and the post-test difference favored the ChatGPT group (4.28 vs. 3.85), t=-2.63, p=.01; no standardized effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Computational Thinking Scale (18-item Likert instrument covering abstraction, decomposition, algorithmic thinking, evaluation, and generalization)
finding.std_deviation: Experimental pre SD=0.76, post SD=0.67; Control pre SD=0.71, post SD=0.91

finding.finding_summary: Students in the comparison condition, who completed the same AI convergence curriculum using search engines and literature information services instead of ChatGPT, showed no statistically significant improvement in computational thinking from pre-test to post-test (M=3.68, SD=0.71 to M=3.85, SD=0.91; t=1.00, p=.32). This suggests that the non-chatbot technology condition did not produce detectable gains on the study’s computational thinking measure over the intervention period.
finding.measure: Computational Thinking Scale (18-item Likert instrument covering abstraction, decomposition, algorithmic thinking, evaluation, and generalization)

finding.finding_summary: The paper frames the intervention as an AI convergence education program embedded in high school subject areas such as convergence science exploration, creative engineering design, and AI basics, and reports significantly stronger overall post-test performance for the ChatGPT group than the control group within this curricular context. However, the measured outcome was computational thinking rather than direct subject-matter attainment, so evidence for academic learning in these domains is indirect.
finding.measure: Computational Thinking Scale used as the study’s proxy outcome within AI convergence education
finding.std_deviation: Experimental post SD=0.67; control post SD=0.91
